en: The God of gods said: In Kurujāṅgala, between the Sarasvatī and the Dṛṣadvatī rivers, [he saw] Lomaharṣaṇa, the ancient and most excellent of sages, seated there.
Then those best of the twice-born inquired about the power of that lake.
Tell me the extent of the lake, and especially of the sacred fords;
tell me the majesty of the deities and the origin of Vāmana.
Having heard these words of theirs, the ancient seer, his hair standing on end with emotion, prostrated himself and spoke these words: VamPSm_1.3 //
Lomaharṣaṇa said:

Having prostrated with my head before Brahmā, the foremost, seated upon his lotus-throne, as well as Viṣṇu accompanied by Lakṣmī, and the god Rudra, I shall describe the great sacred site of Brahmasaras.
"From Rantukādaujasa to Pāvana, a lake was previously declared by Brahmā himself to be situated there. (Vamśastha 1.5)
O best of the twice-born, listen to that measurement of the lake which was proclaimed by the high-souled Vyāsa during the interval between the Kali and Dvāpara ages.
From Viśveśvara to Asthipura, there is the Rathakanyā and the Jaradgavī;
as far as the Oghavatī is said to extend, so far does the Sannihita lake reach.
O best of the twice-born, listen to that meritorious and greatly augmenting authoritative scripture which was heard by me while being recited to Vāmana.
From Viśveśvara, the best of gods and protector of kings, Sarasvatī flows;
the lake known as Saṃnihita should be understood to extend for one yojana in every direction.
Relying upon this, the gods and sages have gathered together;
some serve it for the sake of the desire for liberation, while others remain established for the sake of heaven.
This [place] was resorted to by Brahmā, the yogi desiring to create;
it was resorted to by Viṣṇu in his form as Hari, desiring to maintain [the world].
And having entered the middle of Lake Rudra, the great-souled Hara,
possessed of great splendor, served that sacred ford and attained the state of Sthāṇu.
This was first the altar of Brahmā; from that, it is remembered as the Heart of Rāma (Rāmahṛda);
and because compassion was drawn forth from there, it is therefore remembered as Kurukṣetra.
The space between Tarantuka and Arantuka, and that which lies between Rāmahrada and Caturmukha—
this Kurukṣetra, known as Samantapañcaka, is called the northern altar of the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Thus ends the first chapter in the Śrī Vāmana Purāṇa, concerning the Greatness of Sara.
The sages said:
"Tell us the greatness of Vāmana and his specific origin."
Just as Bali was bound and the kingdom was given to Śatakratu.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
"Listen with pleasure, O sages, to the birth, the power, and the dwelling place in Kurujāṅgala of the high-souled Vāmana."
O best of the twice-born, listen now to that very lineage of the Daityas,
in whose family Bali, the son of Virocana, was born in ancient times.
In ancient times, Hiraṇyakaśipu was the first among the Daityas;
his son was the Dānava named Prahlāda, who possessed great splendor.
From him Virocana was born, and from Virocana Bali was born;
after Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain, [Bali] drove the gods away from all sides.
He ruled the kingdom and performed sacrifices throughout the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile;
while the gods exerted themselves, the three worlds fell into the state of being possessed by Daityas.
When Jaya and the powerful Maya-Śambara were likewise [conquered],
and when all the directions were pure and the practice of dharma had commenced.
When the path of the Daityas had opened and the sun was situated in its southern course,
it was indeed through the counter-incantations of Prahlāda, Śambara, and Maya.
While all the quarters were asleep and the sky was protected by the Daityas, and while the gods displayed the splendor of their sacrifices situated in heaven; ||| VamPSm_2.9 |||
Then, while the world remained in its natural state and on the path of the virtuous,
all evils ceased to exist and the presence of Dharma was ever-arisen.
When the Dharma stands upon four feet, with its limbs consisting of both dharma and adharma;
when kings shine while engaged in the protection of their subjects;
and likewise when those dwelling in the stages of life (āśrama) are devoted to their own respective duties.
Then Bali was consecrated in the sovereignty of the Daityas by all the asuras,
while the hosts of asuras were joyful, shouting, and delighted.
Then Lakṣmī, possessing the luster of the interior of a lotus, with her hand raised holding a lotus, the goddess who grants boons and is easy to enter, accepted the offering. VamPSm 2.13.
Śrī said: "O Bala, best among the powerful, O king of the Daityas, O you of great splendor!
I am pleased with you; may it be well with you for having defeated the king of the gods."
"Because you have conquered the kingdom of the gods through your prowess in battle,
and having witnessed your supreme courage, I have come here in person."
O tiger among dānavas, it is no wonder that such self-restraint as this is found in you, the lord of the asuras, born in the lineage of Hiraṇyakaśipu.
O King, you have distinguished that lord of the Daityas as your great-grandfather,
by whom indeed this entire, imperishable triple-world was enjoyed.
Having spoken thus to Bali, the king of the Daityas, the goddess Lakṣmī—
the giver of boons, the one to be served, and the delight of all the gods— entered [the earth].
And the excellent goddesses were pleased: Hrī, Kīrti, Dyuti, Prabhā, Dhṛti, Kṣamā, Bhūti, Ṛddhi, Divyā, and Mahāmati.
Śruti, Smṛti, Iḍā, Kīrti, Śānti, Puṣṭi, and likewise Kriyā—
all these divine Apsarases are experts in dance and song.
The three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, sought refuge with the lord of the Daityas,
who had attained incomparable sovereignty through his strength and his status as a knower of Brahman.
Thus ends the second chapter, on the Greatness of Sara, in the Kṣīvāma Purāṇa.
The sages said:
"Tell us the deeds of the gods; how was it that they were defeated?"
How did that Viṣṇu, the god beyond gods, assume the form of a dwarf?
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Seeing the three worlds held captive by Bali, the god Purandara,
Śakra, went to the auspicious abode of his mother on a ridge of Mount Meru.
Having approached his mother, he related those words concerning how the Ādityas had been defeated in battle by the Dānava.
Aditi said:
"If it is thus, my sons, that Bali, the son of Virocana, cannot be slain by you all in battle, nor even by all the hosts of Maruts; [then what can be done]?"
O Thousand-eyed One, he can only be slain in battle by one with a thousand heads; for he cannot be slain by anyone else.
In that same manner, I shall question my father Kaśyapa, the expounder of Brahman,
for the sake of defeating that great-souled Daitya Bali.
Then the gods, together with Aditi, arrived in the presence of Kaśyapa;
there they beheld the sage Mārīca, a blazing treasury of ascetic power.
The primordial, divine teacher of the gods, blazing with the splendor of Brahman, having the form of the sun by his brilliance, and resembling a crest of fire; VamPSm_3.8 //
Having laid aside the staff, endowed with asceticism, wearing a bound black antelope skin as his garment,
and clothed in bark and deerskin, he blazed, as it were, with spiritual splendor.
Resembling a blazing fire, preceded by the fragrance of clarified butter,
his father was devoted to sacred study and appeared like a corporeal flame.
To Kaśyapa, the teacher of gods and asuras, the Lord who speaks of Brahman and speaks the truth,
who is peerless in his brahminhood and radiant with splendor through his majesty.
He who is the creator of all worlds, the supreme lord of creatures,
the third Prajāpati by distinction of his own being.
Then, having prostrated themselves, all those heroes— the bulls among the gods together with the Ādityas— spoke with palms joined in reverence, like the mind-born sons of Brahmā.
"The Daitya Bali is invincible in battle even by Śakra and is superior in strength;
therefore, ordain for us that which is beneficial and increases the prosperity of the gods."
Having heard those words of his sons, the lord Kaśyapa,
the creator of the worlds, set his mind upon departing for the world of Brahmā.
Kaśyapa said:
"O Śakra, let us go to the most wonderful abode of Brahmā;
thus we are all prepared to report our defeat to Brahmā."
Then, together with the Ādityas, the gods went from there to the hermitage of Kāśyapa and set out for the abode of Brahmā, which is frequented by hosts of great seers.
In a mere moment, those of great strength and radiant splendor reached the world of Brahmā, traveling in divine vehicles that move at will according to their merit.
Desiring to see Brahmā, the mass of asceticism and the unchanging,
they reached the vast and supreme assembly hall of Brahmā.
Seeing that [song], which was sweet with the humming of bees, chanted by the Sāma-singers, auspicious, and destructive of enemies, they then rejoiced.

The tigers among the gods heard the Ṛgvedic verses— expounded by the leaders of the Bahvṛcas, arranged according to their sequence, words, and syllables— during the performance of the extensive rituals.
Those who were knowers of the science of sacrifice and the Vedas, as well as those who knew the *pada* and *krama* recitations,
caused that assembly to resound with the accents of the supreme sages.
And by twice-born ones who are experts in the praise of sacrifice, as well as those learned in phonetics,
who know the meaning of the meters, and who are proficient in all branches of knowledge.
And there, O best of brahmins, those disciplined ones of celebrated vows heard the sound uttered by the leaders of the Lokāyatas in various places.
The sons of Kaśyapa saw her, who was devoted to recitation and burnt offerings;
in that assembly sat Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds.
The illustrious preceptor of the gods and asuras, by means of his knowledge consisting of the illusory power of the Vedas,
was honored right there by the lords of creatures.
Dakṣa, Pracetas, Pulaha, and Marīci—these are the best of the twice-born;
as well as Bhṛgu, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, and Nārada.
Likewise, knowledge, the intermediate space, wind, fire, water, and earth;
as well as sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.
Nature and its transformations, whatever other great cause there may be, the four Vedas with their limbs and sub-limbs, and likewise the Lord of the World; 3.29.
The methods, the sacrifices, resolve, and even the vital breath—
these and many others worship the Self-Existent One.
Artha, Dharma, Kāma, Krodha, and Harṣa were always present;
as were Śukra, Bṛhaspati, Saṃvarta, and likewise Budha.
Śanaiścara, Rāhu, and all the other planets are established there,
as well as the Maruts, Viśvakarman, and the Vasus, O best of the twice-born.
The sun and the moon, day and night as well,
the half-months and the months, and the six seasons are established there.
Having entered that divine assembly hall of Brahmā, which fulfills all desires,
Kaśyapa— the best among the upholders of dharma— was together with the gods and his sons.
It was composed entirely of splendor, divine, frequented by hosts of Brahman-sages,
attended by the glory of Brahmā, inconceivable, and free from weariness.
Having questioned Brahmā as he sat upon his supreme throne, all those gods,
together with the celestial rishis, bowed their heads in salutation to the Lord.
Then, having bowed at the feet of the Supreme Self,
they were self-restrained, liberated from all sins, peaceful, and cleansed of impurity.
Having seen all those gods who had arrived together with Kaśyapa,
the Lord and Sovereign of the gods, possessed of great majesty, spoke to Brahmā.
Brahmā said:
"O you of great strength, I too shall first consider that purpose for which all of you have indeed arrived here."
"And all that you desire shall come to pass, O best of gods;
he who shall become the conqueror of this Bali, the chief of the Dānavas."
That creator of the universe is not only the goal for the gods and others;
he is the leader of the three worlds and the sovereign even of the deities.
He who is the lord of all worlds and the eternal Lord of the Universe—
him they always call the Primordial God (Ādideva), the eternal First-born.
Even the gods do not know that high-souled one, thinking "Who is he?
Yet that Supreme Person knows us, the gods, the sacred revelation, and the entire universe.
But by his very grace, I shall proclaim the supreme goal,
wherein one, established in yoga, practices austerities difficult to perform.
On the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk, in the northern direction, the Creator of All has established the supreme abode named Amṛta; so say the wise.
Having gone there, you who are praised for your vows,
having reached that immortal abode, perform difficult austerities through penance.
Then you shall hear that resonant sound, smooth and deep,
like the roar of a water-laden cloud at the end of the hot season.
She is red in color, her syllables are full and beautiful, she is always auspicious and bestows fearlessness;
she is Speech, the supreme refinement of those who speak as exponents of Brahman.
Then, for that one of purified soul, [he heard] the divine, truth-effecting, true mantra of the Supreme God of all gods, which destroys all impurities.
Upon the completion of his vow, at the conclusion of the yoga-vow,
that [gift] of the high-souled god Viśvatejas becomes unfailing for him.
"To whom shall I grant what boon? O gods, I stand here as the giver of boons. Welcome to you, O best of deities, who have come into my presence."
Then Aditi and Kaśyapa,
having bowed their heads at the feet of that wise god, should receive the boon.
"May the Blessed One himself become our son; be gracious to us.
When addressed with such supreme words, he will say, "So be it."
"All those gods— Kaśyapa, Aditi,
and all the deities— said to the Lord, 'So be it,' and bowing their heads,
they departed toward the northern direction, heading for Śvetadvīpa."
In no time at all, they reached the Ocean of Milk, the lord of rivers,
exactly as it had been pointed out by the blessed Brahmā, the speaker of truth.
Those best of gods traversed all the oceans, the mountains together with their forests,
and the various divine rivers upon the earth.
They beheld a terrible darkness, devoid of all living beings,
sunless, boundless, and enveloped on all sides by gloom.
Having reached the immortal abode, the high-souled Kaśyapa initiated them into a divine vow that grants all desires for a thousand years.
For the sake of propitiating that lord of the gods, for that wise one who is Yoga itself,
for the divine Nārāyaṇa, the thousand-eyed one, for the sake of prosperity.
Through celibacy, silence, and the hero’s posture,
all the gods gradually undertook fierce asceticism.
There, for the sake of inspiring faith in that Great-Souled One, the Blessed Kaśyapa uttered the supreme hymn declared in the Vedas.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Śrī Vāmana Purāṇa, in the section on the Greatness of Sara.
Kaśyapa said:
"Obeisance be to You, O God of gods, O One-horned One, O You who are worshipped by the Bull (Śiva), O Bull of the Ocean, O Vṛṣākapi, O Bull among the gods, O You who are without beginning!"

O Rudra, Kapila, Viṣvaksena, Lord of all beings, Dhruva, Dharma-adharma, Vaikuṇṭha, Vṛṣāvarta, you who are without beginning, middle, or end, Dhanañjaya, Śuciśravas, Pṛśnitejas, Nijaya, (5) Amṛteśaya, Sanātana, Tridhāman, Tuṣita, Mahātattva, Lokanātha, Padmanābha, Viriñci, Bahurūpa!
Akṣaya, Akṣara, Havyabhuj, Khaṇḍaparaśu, Śatakratu, Muñjakeśa, Haṃsa, Mahādakṣiṇa, Hṛṣīkeśa,
Sūkṣma, Mahāniyamadhara, Viraja, Lokapratiṣṭha, Arūpa, Agraja, Dharmaja, Dharmanābha,
Gabhastinābha, Śatakratunābha, Candraratha, Sūryatejas, Samudravāsa, Aja, Sahasraśiras. (10)
O thousand-footed one, downward-faced one, Great Person, Supreme Person; O thousand-armed one, thousand-formed one, thousand-faced one, Supreme Person;
O thousand-armed one, thousand-formed one, thousand-faced one, born of a thousand, they call you the essence of a thousand beings.
O Puṣpahāsa, O Carama, you alone are Vauṣaṭ;
they call you Vaṣaṭkāra, the foremost in sacrifices, the partaker of the oblation, and the one with a thousand streams. You alone are Bhuḥ, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ;
you are the one to be known through the Vedas, the one who lies within Brahman, and the beloved of the Brāhmaṇas. You alone are the sky, you are Mātariśvan, and you are Dharma.

You alone are the Hotṛ, the Potṛ, the thinker, the leader, and the cause of the oblation; O foremost one, you alone exist through all abodes. You alone are the quarters together with the auspicious vessels;
you are the object of worship, you are the wise one, and you alone are the fuel, the intellect, the goal, and the giver.
You are liberation; you are yoga.
You create;
you are the Ordainer, you are the supreme sacrifice, you are Soma, you are the consecrated one, you are the sacrificial fee, you are the universe.
O Ancient One, whose name is Gold, Nārāyaṇa, the three-eyed one, whose armor is the sun, whose splendor is the sun, the Great Person. (25)

O Supreme Person, primordial deity, of noble strides, maker of light, O Śambhu, self-existent one, origin of beings, you are the great being, the being of the universe; you alone are the universe, the protector of the universe, the purifier, the source of all things, the one whose actions are directed upward, the immortal Lord of Heaven,
Lord of Speech, you whose radiance is clarified butter, you of infinite deeds, O Pra-gvaṃśa, you alone are the protector of the universe and the giver of boons to those who seek them.
(30) "To you who are offered oblations by four, by four, by two, and indeed by five,
and again by two— you, whose nature is the Hotṛ priest, salutations!
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Śrī Vāmana Purāṇa, in the section on the Greatness of Saramā.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
But the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, having heard this supreme hymn uttered by Kaśyapa, the best of the twice-born and a knower of Brahman, [was moved].
The illustrious Lord, the Sovereign, being satisfied and delighted in mind, spoke these words correctly, with full and resonant syllables, just as a master speaks.
"Choose a boon; may it be well with you! I am the giver of boons, O best of gods.
Kaśyapa said:
"O best of gods, you are pleased with us; this is the unanimous resolve of us all."
The younger brother of Vāsava, the increaser of the joy of his kinsmen,
the illustrious and blessed son of Aditi, has indeed set.
And Aditi, the mother of the gods, seeking a boon, spoke this very same supreme matter for the sake of a son to the Blessed One, the granter of boons. (VamPSm 6.5)
The gods said: O Maheśvara, for the sake of the ultimate welfare of all deities,
be forever our protector, sustainer, giver, and refuge.
Then Viṣṇu spoke to those gods and to Kaśyapa:
"All those who shall be your enemies,
none of them shall remain before me even for a moment."
Having slain all the hosts of Asuras who partake of the first portions of the sacrificial offerings,
as well as all the gods who consume the *havya* and even the ancestors who consume the *kavya*.
"O best of the wise, I shall perform the rite for the supreme state;
O most excellent gods, return by the same path by which you came."
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
When this had been spoken by the powerful Lord Viṣṇu,
they, with delighted minds, then worshipped that Lord.
The Viśvedevas, the high-souled Kaśyapa, and Aditi,
having paid homage with speed to that god, the Lord of the Suras, [proceeded].
They all set out toward the eastern direction for the vast hermitage of Kaśyapa;
having reached Kaśyapa’s hermitage, they proceeded to the great forest of Kurukṣetra.
Having propitiated Aditi there, they directed her toward asceticism;
then she performed severe penance for ten thousand years.
In order to propitiate Kṛṣṇa, she— whose speech was conquered and who subsisted on air— created a divine, auspicious forest that grants all desires, which was named after her.
Seeing her sons rejected by the Daityas, that best of sages said,
"I am one whose son is in vain. Out of despondency and with devotion,
she praised Hari with foremost words that awaken the knowledge of the supreme truth.
They bowed down to Viṣṇu, the refuge and protector who is compassionate toward his devotees,
who consists of gods and demons, and whose nature is without beginning, middle, or end.
Aditi said:
"Salutations to the destroyer of the affliction caused by magic spells; salutations to the one garlanded with lotuses;
salutations to the supreme auspiciousness, the auspicious one, the primordial creator."
Homage to the lotus-eyed one; homage to the one whose navel is a lotus;
homage to the self-born one, the source of the birth of the lotus.
Salutation to the beloved of Śrī, the self-controlled one, who is visible to those who have mastered their senses, the wielder of the discus;
salutation to him whose hand holds the lotus and the sword, salutation to the one whose seed is gold.

Likewise, [salutations] to Hari, who is the sacrifice of self-knowledge, who is to be contemplated by yogis, who is the yogi, who is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), who is the ultimate distinction, and whose form is Brahman.
Salutations to that divine wielder of the Śārṅga bow, who is both gross and exceedingly subtle, in whom the world abides, yet who is not seen by the world.
That which people do not see even while seeing the entire world,
and that which is seen by those who do not see the world, abides within the heart.
That which is perceived as external light, yet is beyond light and cannot be defined;
that in which this entire universe exists, from which it arises, and to which it belongs.
Salutations again and again to him, the immortal one of all the worlds;
he who is the first Prajāpati and the supreme lord of the ancestors,
the lord of the gods— to that Kṛṣṇa, the creator, [be] salutation.
Salutations to that wielder of the mace, who bestows the fruits of heaven and liberation, and through whom one becomes detached from action, whether it be engaged or withdrawn.
Salutations to that pure, supreme Hari-megha, who dispels all evil even when he is merely being meditated upon.
I bow to that Lord, the unborn and imperishable support of all, whom those who behold no longer undergo birth and death.
I bow to that Lord Viṣṇu, the master and sovereign, who is the sacrifice itself, established in sacrifice, and who is worshipped by those for whom sacrifice is supreme.
Salutation to that eternal Viṣṇu, the goal of the wise, who is sung of in all the Vedas by those who know the Vedas, and who is to be known through the Vedas.
Salutations to that Great Soul, from whom the universe has arisen and into whom it shall go to its dissolution; salutations to the source and foundation of the universe.
I bow to that Upendra, by whom the moving and unmoving world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, is pervaded and bound together by the net of Māyā.
I bow to that Lord Prajāpati, Viṣṇu, the master of the universe, who, abiding here in the very nature of water, sustains the entire world.
I bow to that Upendra, who, in the form of the sun, destroys the embodied demon Tamas of that kind born of the night.
I bow down to that Upendra, whose eyes are the sun and the moon, who constantly beholds the good and evil deeds of all the worlds.
I bow to that unborn Viṣṇu, the source and the imperishable, in whom— O Lord of all— all this that has been spoken by me is true, and not false.
O Janārdana, if what I have spoken here is true,
then by that truth, may all my heart's desires be fulfilled once again.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Śrī Vāmana Purāṇa, concerning the Greatness of Sara.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Having been thus praised, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva then spoke to her.
Invisible to all beings, he remained within her sight.
The Blessed One said: "O Aditi, whatever desires you wish for, those you shall obtain through my grace, O knower of dharma; of this there is no doubt."
Listen, O highly fortunate lady, to the boon that resides in your heart;
for my sight shall never be in vain.
And whoever, staying here in your forest, shall observe the three-night vow,
all their desires will be fulfilled— whatever they wish for here with their mind.
Even a man who, though staying far away, remembers the forest of Aditi, goes to the supreme abode; how much more so a man who actually dwells there?
And whoever here, endowed with faith, should feed five, three, two, or even just one Brahmin, he goes to the supreme goal.
Aditi said:
"O God, you who are compassionate toward your devotees, if you are pleased with my devotion,
then let Vāsava be my son, the sovereign of the three worlds."
His kingdom has been seized and his share of the sacrifice taken here by the asuras;
O Supreme One, when you are pleased, let my son regain that.
"O Keśava, the loss of my son's kingdom does not cause me such grief as the deprivation of the inheritance granted to him; that seizure causes me torment."
The Blessed One said: "O Goddess, I have indeed shown you favor according to your desire;
by means of my own portion, I shall be conceived in your womb through Kaśyapa."
Those who have arisen from your womb and those who are your swift-moving attendants, I shall slay them all; turn back, O joyful one!
Aditi said:
"Be gracious, O Lord of the gods; salutations to you, O Creator of the universe!
O Keśava, I am not able to carry you within my womb."
In whom everything is established, you are the Lord, the source of the universe.
"I shall carry you and myself as well, O Nandinī;
I will cause you no distress. May it be well with you; I am departing."
When the god had vanished after speaking thus, Aditi conceived a fetus.
While Kṛṣṇa was situated within the womb, the broad earth trembled;
the great mountains shook, and the vast oceans were thrown into agitation.
O best of the twice-born, wherever Aditi went, she offered her supreme foot; from those very places, the earth bowed down out of weariness.
While Madhusūdana was still in the womb, the luster of all the Daityas also diminished, exactly as had been declared by the Supreme Lord.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Śrī Vāmana Purāṇa, in the section on the Greatness of Sara.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Having seen all the Asuras slain, the Lord of the Asuras [beheld] them.
Then Bali questioned Prahlāda, his own grandfather.
Bali said:
"O father, these Daityas are devoid of luster, as if consumed by fire;
why are they all of a sudden today like those struck by the staff of Brahmā?"
What ill-omened rite was performed by the Daityas, or what *kṛtyā* created by fate has arisen for their destruction, by which the Asuras have been deprived of their splendor?
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
O Brāhmaṇas, having been thus questioned by his grandson,
that best of Asuras reflected for a long time and then spoke these words to the Asura Bali.
Prahlāda said:
The mountains are shaking, the earth suddenly loses its firmness,
the oceans are instantly agitated, and the Daityas have been rendered lusterless.
The planets do not move as they did previously at sunrise;
the supreme fortune of the gods is inferred by means of the *karaṇa*.
"This is a great matter, O mighty-armed lord of the Dānavas;
you must by no means consider it to be a trivial task."
Lomaharṣaṇa said: Having spoken thus to the lord of the Dānavas, that Prahlāda, the best of Asuras,
being exceedingly devoted to the Lord of Gods, went in his mind to Hari.
Having brought his mind onto the path of meditation, the asura Prahlāda then reflected upon how the god Janārdana was situated.
He saw Prahlāda in the form of a dwarf within the belly of Aditi,
and therein also the Vasus, the Rudras, the Aśvins, and the Maruts.
[He conquered] the Sādhyas, as well as the Viśvedevas, the Ādityas, the Gandharvas, the Uragas, and the Rākṣasas;
and Virocana, the son [of Prahlāda], and Bali, the leader of the Asuras.
Jambha, Kujambha, Naraka, Bāṇa, and likewise other asuras;
himself, the earth, the sky, wind, water, and fire.
He beheld the oceans, mountains, rivers, and islands, as well as lakes, cattle, the earth,
all birds and humans, and likewise all reptiles.
[He saw] Brahmā, the creator of all the worlds, as well as Bhava himself,
the planets, the lunar mansions, and the stars, and the patriarchs beginning with Dakṣa.
Beholding this, overcome with wonder yet returning to his natural state in an instant, Prahlāda then spoke to Bali, the lord of the Daityas and son of Virocana: VamPSm_8.15 //
I shall relate all that which has caused this loss of splendor to arise for you; listen to it in its entirety.
The god of gods, the source of the world, unborn, the first-born of the world; beginningless, the origin of the universe, the most excellent, the giver of boons—Hari.
The supreme among the high and the low, the goal of those who are both high and low,
the Lord, the authority of all authorities, and the teacher of the teacher of the seven worlds—
that inconceivable Lord of the Universe entered the state of being in a womb in order to establish the stability of the world.
The Lord of lords, the supreme among the highest, the Blessed One who is without beginning or middle, the infinite one—
the Great-Souled Aditi-born has descended as a single portion to provide a protector for the three worlds.
O Lord of Daityas, he whose true nature neither Rudra, nor the lotus-born Brahmā, nor Indra, nor the sun, moon, and their rays know— that Vāsudeva has descended with a portion of himself.

I bow down to that god Vāsudeva, whom those learned in the Vedas call the "Imperishable Syllable" (Yamakṣara), into whom those whose sins have been shaken off by knowledge enter, and having entered whom they are not born again.

I bow down to that inconceivable Vāsudeva, from whom all things without exception arise incessantly like waves from the ocean, and into whom they go to their dissolution at the time of the final absorption.
I perpetually bow down to that Vāsudeva, whose form, strength, power, and majesty are not known even by the Grandfather and all others, he who is the Supreme Person.

The eye is for the perception of form, this skin is the grasper of touch, the tongue is for taste, and the nose is appointed for the perception of smell; the nose, eye, ear, and so forth are not [the perceivers] of that [smell].
He who is self-luminous and the Lord of all in the ultimate sense is to be known through reasoning;
I bow to that Hari, the adorable and sinless God, the Grasper and Sovereign.

I bow down to that Lord Viṣṇu, who is worthy of praise, by whom this earth with its mountains was lifted up with a single tusk and now sustains everything here; and he who, having swallowed the entire world, lies asleep.
I bow to that infinite Lord, the God who, having descended as a partial incarnation, withdrew the splendors of the great asuras within the womb; he is the axe for the entire tree of saṃsāra.

O great lords of the asuras, this Great-Souled One, the divine source of the universe, entered the womb of the mother of the lord of the gods with his sixteenth part; by him, your strength and bodies were taken away.
Bali said:
"Father, who is this one named Hari from whom this fear has come upon us?
I have hundreds of Daityas here whose strength exceeds that of Vāsudeva."
Vipracitti, Śibi, Śaṅku, Aya, and likewise Śaṅku;
Hayaśiras, Aśvaśiras, Bhaṅgakāra, and Mahāhanu.
Pratāpin, Praghasa, Śambhu, Kukkurākṣa, and Durjaya—
these and other Daityas and Dānavas are mine.
Possessing great strength and great heroism, they are capable of bearing the burden of the earth;
Kṛṣṇa is not equal to even half the prowess of each one of them individually.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Having heard these words of his grandson, Prahlāda, the best of the Daityas,
spoke with anger to Bali, who had spoken in reproach of Vaikuṇṭha.
The Daityas and those Dānavas as well shall meet their destruction,
they who have such a king as you— one of evil intellect and lacking discernment.
"O one of sinful intent, who else besides you would speak thus of the God of gods, the highly fortunate Vāsudeva, the unborn and all-pervading Lord?"
All these Daityas and Dānavas whom you have mentioned, as well as the gods including Brahmā, and all manifestations down to the stationary beings— VamPSm_8.36.
Both you and I, and this entire world—with its mountains, trees, rivers, and forests; this world with its oceans and islands; and all that is moving and unmoving—[are but a reflection].
Who can thus describe him— the pervasive Supreme Self, who is to be saluted and worshipped, and whose birth is but a minute fraction of a portion of a single part?
Except for you alone— devoid of discernment, evil-minded, with an unsubdued self, aged, and transgressing the teachings— who are intent upon destruction.
I am to be pitied, for in my house was born your base father,
who had such a son as you— a despiser of the God of gods.
Let alone devotion to Kṛṣṇa, who destroys the flood of the multitude of many saṃsāras; must I not be looked after by you for now?
"This body of mine is dearer to me even than Kṛṣṇa"—
this is what the world knows, and you too, O son of Diti.
Although you know that Hari is dearer to me than even my own life, you still revile him; by doing so, you show no respect for me.
"Virocana was your teacher, and I am your teacher as well, O Bali;
yet for me too, Nārāyaṇa Hari is the teacher of all the worlds."
Since you have uttered censure against Kṛṣṇa— the teacher of teachers— you shall,
for that reason, fall from your sovereignty even in this very life.
That god, the lord of the worlds, the master of strength, Janārdana—surely you must look after me, for I am devoted to him; he is my teacher in this matter.
"Since you have not shown due regard for the Teacher of the World by censuring him for even this much, therefore I pronounce a curse upon you."
"O Bala, since you have spoken this insult against Acyuta—which to me is even weightier than the severing of my head—fall down, deprived of your kingdom! (Vamśastha 8.48)
Just as there is no protector other than Kṛṣṇa in the ocean of existence,
so may I soon behold you fallen from your kingdom.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, on the Greatness of Sara, in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Having heard these harsh and unpleasant words, the lord of the Daityas—
Having prostrated again and again, he sought to please his teacher.
Bali said:
"Be gracious, father; do not be angry with me, who am struck by delusion.
This speech was uttered by me while I was deluded by the arrogance of my own strength."
O best of the Daityas, I am a sinner whose consciousness has been struck down by delusion;
that I, a man of evil conduct, have been cursed—this which you have done is well.
"O dear one, just as you are despondent thinking, 'I shall suffer the loss of my kingdom and the loss of my fame,' so too would it be if misconduct were committed."
Sovereignty over the three worlds, lordship, or anything else is not very difficult to obtain;
but in this world, O dear one, teachers such as you are rare to find.
Be gracious, O father; you ought not to be angry, O Lord of Daityas.
Scorched by your anger, I burn with anguish day and night.
Prahlāda said: "O child, through my anger, delusion was produced;
because of that, the curse was given by me to you, and discrimination was taken away from me by that delusion."
O great asura, if my knowledge had not been eclipsed by delusion,
how could I, knowing Hari to be omnipresent, ever cast a glance at him?
"O foremost of asuras, whatever curse has been pronounced by me upon you must surely come to pass;
therefore, do not despair."
"From this day forward, O Lord of Gods, you must be devoted to the Blessed One, Hari, the Imperishable Lord; he shall be your protector."
O hero, since you have remembered the Lord of Gods after receiving my curse,
I shall speak in such a way that you will attain your own welfare.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Having obtained the boon that fulfills all desires,
the highly illustrious god gradually attained growth within her womb.
Then, when the tenth month had arrived and the time for birth came,
that Blessed One Govinda was born in the form of a dwarf.
When that Lord of the World, the sovereign of all the immortals, had descended,
the gods and Aditi, the mother of the gods, likewise released their sorrow.
The winds blew with pleasant touch, the sky became free from dust,
and at that time, the minds of all living beings turned toward righteousness.
O best of the twice-born, there was no agitation in the bodies of men;
for at that time, the minds of all beings were directed toward dharma.
As soon as he was born, the Blessed One Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds,
performed the birth rites and other ceremonies, and praised the Lord.
Brahmā said:
Victory, O Lord! Victory, O unconquerable one! Victory, O Teacher of the Universe, O Hari!
Victory, O Infinite One who transcends birth, death, and old age! Victory, O Acyuta!
Victory to you, the unconquered! Victory to you, the one who has conquered all! Victory to you, who abide in the unmanifest! Victory!
O Omniscient One, whose purpose is the ultimate truth, who have emerged from the objects of knowledge and the means of knowledge!
Victory to you, the witness of the entire world, the creator of the world, the teacher of the world!
O Lord who is both beyond the world and its end, victory to you who protects the world during its duration!
Victory to you, O All-encompassing One! Victory to you, O Entirety! Victory to you, who dwell in the hearts of all!
Victory to you, who consist of the beginning, middle, and end, the supreme embodiment of all knowledge!

O Lord, who are indefinable by those seeking liberation, eternally joyful, victorious, and adorned with the virtues of self-restraint and other qualities cherished by yogis desiring emancipation! VamPSm_9.22 //
Victory to you, O most subtle one, difficult to know; victory to you, O gross one, who pervades the universe!
Victory to you, O subtler than the subtle; victory to you, who are both beyond the senses and possessed of the senses!
Victory to you who abide in the yoga of your own māyā, O Śeṣa, the Enjoyer; victory to you, the Imperishable One!
Victory to you who lifted up the earth with the tip of your single tusk! VamPSm_9.24 //
O Man-lion, O rending of the chest of the enemy of the gods,
conquer now, O Soul of the Universe, O Māyā-Vāmana, O Keśava!
O Janārdana, sustainer of the world delimited by Your own māyā! Victory to You, the inconceivable! Victory to You, O Lord who are of a single nature despite manifold forms! VamPSm 9.26.
Prosper, O Hari, you whose nature consists of manifold transformations that have been increased;
in you, the Lord of the worlds, this path of dharma is established.
O Hari, neither I, nor Īśāna, nor Indra and the other gods,
nor the sages such as Sanaka, nor the yogis are able to know you.
O Lord of the World, you are veiled by the cloth of illusion in this world;
O Sovereign of All, what man can know you without your grace?
O Lord, he alone by whom you have been propitiated and whose face you favor with grace knows you as a god; no other knows you, O Unborn One.
O Lord of the lords of lords, O Sovereign, O All-pervading One, O Creator, increase for the sake of the manifestation of this universe, O Universal Self, O Large-eyed One!
Lomaharṣaṇa said: Thus praised, Hṛṣīkeśa, who had assumed the form of a dwarf,
then laughed and spoke with profound gravity to him whose prosperity was now fully attained.
"I was previously praised by you, by Indra and the others, and by Kaśyapa;
and I promised you the three worlds for Indra."
Furthermore, I was praised by Aditi,
and from her I heard how I would bestow the three worlds, cleared of all thorns, upon Śakra.
Therefore, I shall act in such a way that Indra will become the thousand-eyed lord of the world; I tell you this as the truth.
Then he gave a black antelope skin to Brahmā Hṛṣīkeśa;
the Lord Bṛhaspati gave him a sacred thread.
Marīci, the son of Brahmā, gave the staff to Āṣāḍha; Vasiṣṭha gave the water-pot; Aṅgiras gave the hempen bark garment;
Pulaha gave the seat; and Pulastya gave two yellow robes.
The Vedas, adorned with the sound of the *praṇava*, stood before him,
as did all the scriptures without exception, as well as the teachings of Sāṃkhya and Yoga.
That dwarf god, possessing matted hair, a staff, and an umbrella, and holding a water-pot,
who embodies all the gods, approached the sacrifice of Bali.
Wherever Vāmana set his foot upon the ground, O brahmins,
the earth, being pressed down, gave way there at every spot.
That dwarf, moving slowly with a gait like that of a dull-witted man, caused the entire earth— with its mountains, oceans,
and islands, and its boundaries— to tremble.
But Bṛhaspati slowly showed him the auspicious path;
thus, for the sake of playful diversion, he became exceedingly dull-witted.
Then that great serpent Śeṣa, having emerged from the netherworld (rasātala),
rendered assistance to the Discus-wielder, the God of gods.
Even today, that supreme cave of the renowned great serpent remains famous;
by the mere sight of it, no fear arises from the *nāgas*.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Śrī Vāmana Purāṇa, concerning the Greatness of Sara.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Having seen the earth, together with its mountains and forests, agitated, Bali—
Having prostrated with palms joined in reverence, he questioned Śukra, the son of Uśanas.
O Teacher, the earth with its oceans and mountains is being agitated;
and why is it that the sacrificial fires do not accept their portions from the asuras?
Thus questioned by Bali, the highly intelligent Kāvya, the best among the knowers of the Vedas,
spoke to the lord of the Daityas after reflecting for a long time.
The eternal Supreme Self, Hari, the source of the universe, descended here into the house of Kaśyapa in the form of a dwarf.
"He is surely coming to your sacrifice, O bull among the Dānavas;
it is from the agitation caused by his footsteps that this earth has trembled."
These mountains tremble and the oceans are agitated;
this earth is not capable of supporting the Lord, the Master of Beings.
Together with the gods, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas,
the earth, water, fire, wind, and sky are sustained by this very [power];
it sustains all the gods, humans, and great asuras.
This is the profound illusion of Kṛṣṇa,
the sustainer of the world, by which the universe is oppressed through the relationship of the supported and the supporter.
Due to his presence, the Asuras, the enemies of the gods, are no longer entitled to their shares;
for that reason, the three fires do not consume the portions belonging to the Asuras.
Having heard the words of Śukra, Bali, his hair standing on end with joy, said:
"I am blessed and one who has performed meritorious deeds, since the Lord of Sacrifice himself has come to my sacrifice, O Brahmin; what other man could be more fortunate than I?"
"That supreme, imperishable Self whom yogis, ever-diligent,
desire to behold— that God shall come to my sacrifice.
O Teacher, you ought to instruct me in that which must be performed by me."
Śukra said:
"O Asura, by virtue of the authority of the Vedas, the gods are the partakers of the sacrificial offerings;
yet you, O Daitya, have made the Dānavas the partakers of the sacrificial offerings."
And this Lord, established in the quality of goodness (sattva), performs the preservation of the world;
likewise, having emitted [the creatures], this Lord himself consumes them.
But you, O illustrious one, will surely become Viṣṇu, remaining steadfast in your station;
having understood this, do what is in your heart.
O Lord of Daityas, you must certainly not uphold a vow for even a very small matter; rather, conciliation should be spoken, as it yields the desired fruit.

"O great Asura, since the Lord has accomplished his purpose and is acting for the sake of the gods, I shall give you sufficient wealth; however, this must be said only when he himself asks, for Kṛṣṇa is engaged in promoting the prosperity of the gods."
Bali said:
"O Brahmin, how could I say 'it is not' even when requested by another; how much less so in the case of the Lord, the remover of sins, who is my very own?"
Govinda, who is the Lord seized by various vows and fasts, will say to me, "Give [it] to me"— what could be greater than this?
"For what purpose those endowed with the virtues of self-restraint and purity perform sacrifices of great undertaking—that Lord of Sacrifice shall say to me: 'Grant it to me.'"
Therefore, may my virtuous deeds, my well-performed ritual acts,
and my well-practiced asceticism be such that the Lord of All himself will say to me, "Give me [this]."
"O Guru, I shall say 'it does not exist' to that Lord who has arrived;
I will rather give up my life than say 'it does not exist' anywhere among people."
"I did not say 'it does not exist' even when others entreated me; how could I say so now that the imperishable Cāmara has arrived? (Vamśasthavila 10.22)
Indeed, for heroes, even the onset of calamity is praiseworthy through the act of giving;
that gift which does not cause harm is considered a powerful limb of strength.
In my kingdom, there was no one who was unhappy, nor any who was poor, nor any who was diseased;
none were distressed, nor agitated, nor deprived of peace and the like.
O highly fortunate one, every person is joyful, contented, fragrant, satisfied, and endowed with all happiness; how much more so am I, who am always happy?
"I obtain here this distinguished fruit of the seed of giving;
O tiger among sages, this has been understood by me as heard from your own mouth."
Surely Hira, intent upon my grace, has been propitiated by sacrifice;
having obtained my gift, he nourishes the deities.
If this seed of generosity falls upon the Guru,
Janārdana, the most excellent vessel, what then have I not attained?
That gift of mine is distinguished, and the deities are well-pleased;
it is taught that a gift given for the sake of enjoyment produces a hundredfold happiness.
Surely Hari was propitiated by one who was solely intent on my grace;
therefore, he approaches him to bestow favor upon seeing him—of this there is no doubt.
If he approaches in anger because his share as a god has been obstructed,
and seeks to kill me, then death at the hands of Acyuta would be more praiseworthy.
Knowing this, O best of sages, I must not harbor any thought of giving when Govinda, the Lord of the World, has appeared before me as the dispeller of obstacles.
Lomaharṣaṇa said: While he was speaking thus, Janārdana arrived there—
the inconceivable one who embodies all the gods, possessing illusory power and assuming the form of a dwarf.
Seeing that the Lord had entered the sacrificial enclosure, the asuras were shaken by his power and became lusterless before his splendor.
And the sages who had assembled there at that great sacrifice were Jeṣu,
Vasiṣṭha, Gādhija, Garga, and other most excellent sages.
And Bali considered his entire birth to have become fruitful;
thereafter, overcome with agitation, no one said anything at all.
Each one worshipped the Lord of the Gods with their own splendor;
then the excellent sages beheld those lords of the asuras bowing humbly.
The Lord of the gods of gods, Viṣṇu himself, assuming the form of a dwarf,
being thus honored, praised the sacrifice, the fire, and the sacrificer;
he also praised the members of the assembly who were established in their authority over the sacrificial rites and the abundance of ritual materials.
At that very moment, the members of the assembly and the Brahmins stationed in the sacrificial enclosure exclaimed "Excellent! Excellent! toward Vāmana, who was the vessel for all [the offerings].
Then, taking that water of honor (*argha*), the great asura Bali, his hair standing on end with joy, worshipped Govinda and spoke these words.
Bali said:
"A collection of gold and jewels, as well as a multitude of elephants and horses;
women, garments, ornaments, cows, and abundant villages."
"Either all the earth shall belong to you, or whatever else you desire;
grant me that which you wish for, for my wealth is dear to me."
Thus addressed by the lord of the Daityas with words full of affection, the Blessed One, in the form of a dwarf, spoke with a smile and in a deep voice: VamPSm_10.43.
"O King, grant me three paces of land for the purpose of a fire-sanctuary;
let gold, villages, jewels, and other such things be given to those who desire them. (VamPSm 10.44)
Bali said:
"O best among those who possess feet, what need have you for three steps?
You may seek a hundred, or even a hundred thousand, steps."
The venerable Vāmana said:
"O Lord of Daityas, by this much alone I have achieved my purpose in seeking;
you shall give wealth to other supplicants according to their desire."
Having heard these words spoken by the high-souled Vāmana,
he indeed caused them to be recited to that great-souled Vāmana.
When the water fell upon his hand, the dwarf became non-dwarf;
at that very moment, he manifested a form composed of all the gods.
The sun and moon are his two eyes; heaven is his head and the earth his feet;
the piśācas are his toes, and the guhyakas his fingers.
The Viśvedevas reside in the knees, and the Sādhyas, the best of gods, in the shanks;
the Yakṣas are manifested in the nails, and likewise the Apsarases in the lines.
All the stars without exception are the eyes of the Lord; the rays of the sun are his hair;
the stars are the pores of his skin, and within those pores dwell the great ṛṣis.
The intermediate directions were the arms of that Great-Souled One, and the cardinal directions were his ears;
the two Aśvins were the hearing of that Great-Souled One, and Vāyu was his nose.
In his clarity was the god Candramas, and in his mind was Dharma established;
truth became his speech, and the goddess Sarasvatī his tongue.
The neck was Aditi, the mother of the gods; likewise, the earrings were the Vidyās.
The gate of heaven became Maitra, and Tvaṣṭṛ and Pūṣan were indeed the two eyebrows.
Vaiśvānara is in his mouth, Prajāpati in his testicles,
the Supreme Brahman in his heart, and the sage Kaśyapa is indeed his virility.
The Vasu deities reside on his back, and the Maruts in all his joints;
likewise, Rudra is in his chest, and the great ocean is in his fortitude.
In his belly are the Gandharvas and the mighty Maruts;
Lakṣmī, Medhā, Dhṛti, and Kānti are indeed his hips, as are all branches of knowledge.
All the luminaries that exist here, as well as supreme and great austerity,
are the most excellent splendor manifested from that God of gods.
The Vedas are his flanks, the great sacrifices his knees,
the *iṣṭis* and animal sacrifices his [other] limbs, as are the ritual activities of the twice-born.
Having seen that divine form of the high-souled Viṣṇu,
those Daityas rushed toward him like moths into a fire.
The great Daitya Cikṣura seized Hari’s big toe;
Hari, for his part, struck his neck with his teeth and his big toe.
Having crushed all the asuras with the soles of his feet and the palms of his hands,
the Lord assumed a massive form and swiftly reclaimed the earth.
As he strode across the earth, the moon and sun were situated between his breasts;
as he strode through the sky, both remained positioned at the region of his thighs.
As Viṣṇu exerted his supreme prowess while standing engaged in the task of protecting the gods, these two suns remained at the base of his knees.
Having conquered the three worlds and slain those foremost of the Asuras,
Viṣṇu of the wide strides gave the triple world to Purandara.
Below the surface of the earth is the subterranean realm named Sutala,
which was granted to Bali by the powerful Lord Viṣṇu.
Then Viṣṇu, the Lord of all lords, said to the lord of the Daityas:
"The water that was offered by you has been taken up by me with my hand."
Therefore, your supreme lifespan shall be the measure of a kalpa,
even when the Vaivasvata period has passed and during that subsequent manvantara.
"When the Sāvarṇika period arrives, you shall become Indra;
indeed, all the worlds were formerly given to Śakra."
The arrangement of the four ages consists of seventy-one plus some more;
all those who are his adversaries must be restrained by me.
Therefore, O Balarāma, having been previously propitiated by you with supreme devotion,
I have reached the netherworld named Sutala and have spoken these words to you.
O Vasāsura, properly carrying out my command,
go there to that place endowed with divine pleasures and crowded with hundreds of palaces.
In a lake of fully blossomed lotuses, at the mouth of a river pure as the moon,
fragrant and abundant with cakes, he is adorned with excellent ornaments.
O Lord of the Dānavas, with your limbs smeared with garlands, sandalwood paste, and other unguents, you enjoy various great pleasures that are enchanting through dance and song.
By my command, remain in this time surrounded by a hundred women,
as long as you do not come into conflict with the gods and the brahmins.
"For now, enjoy all pleasures endowed with every object of desire;
but when you enter into conflict with the gods and the brahmins,
then the nooses of Varuṇa, terrible to behold, shall bind you."
Bali said:
"O Blessed One, since I am dwelling there in Pātāla by your command,
what means of acquisition will there be for me to provide the necessary objects of enjoyment?"
O Lord, may I, being nourished by this, remember you always.
The Blessed One said:
"Gifts given without following the prescribed rules, funeral rites (*śrāddha*) performed for those who are not learned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*),
and oblations offered without faith— these shall yield their fruit to you."
Likewise, sacrifices without sacrificial fees, rites performed contrary to the rules,
and Vedic studies undertaken without vows will yield fruits for you.
O Bala, whatever rite is performed without water, without darbha grass, and without clarified butter for the oblation, those will yield fruit [even so]. (VamPSm 10.80)
And whoever, relying upon this place, shall perform any rites,
there shall never be any portion for the asuras.
In the highly meritorious Jyeṣṭhāśrama, as well as at Viṣṇupada and Hṛda,
those who shall offer śrāddhas, as well as vows and observances, [shall obtain great merit].
Whatever ritual action has been performed, whether according to the prescribed rules or otherwise, all of that shall become inexhaustible for him; of this there is no doubt.
Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha,
or having bathed at Viṣṇupada on the twelfth day and beheld Vāmana,
one who gives a gift according to their ability attains the supreme state.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Having granted this boon to Bali and the celestial realm to Śakra,
Hari, in that all-pervading form, vanished from sight.
And the powerful Indra ruled the three worlds as before,
while Bali, having been cast down, remained in Pātāla for that entire duration of time.
Thus has this supreme majesty of Viṣṇu as Vāmana been told;
whoever hears it is liberated from all sins.
Those human beings who shall remember the dialogue between Bali and Prahlāda, the counsel of Bali and Śukra, and the life-story of Bali and Viṣṇu;
O best of the twice-born, neither mental anxieties nor physical ailments, nor a mind agitated by delusion, shall ever befall that man.
Having heard this story, O highly fortunate ones, a man who has lost his kingdom shall regain his own kingdom, and one who suffers separation shall attain the fulfillment of his desires.
A Brāhmaṇa attains the Veda, a Kṣatriya conquers the earth,
a Vaiśya achieves abundance of wealth, and a Śūdra obtains happiness; moreover,
by hearing the greatness of Vāmana, one is liberated from sins.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Śrī Vāmana Purāṇa, concerning the majesty of Sara.
The sages said:
"How did this most excellent of rivers originate?"
The highly fortunate Sakakhatī flows toward Kurukṣetra.
"How did she, having reached the lake and established sacred fords (tīrthas) along its sides,
proceed toward the western direction with her auspicious movement appearing and disappearing?
Tell me this in detail— the eternal lineage of the sacred fords."
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
The eternal and most excellent river, which originates from the Plakṣa tree,

you, O Goddess, are the supreme imperishable (akṣara) in whom everything is established.

Just as fire resides permanently in wood and fragrance in the earth,
so too does Brahman abide within you, and this entire world without exception.
O Goddess, that which is the abiding state of the syllable Oṃ is both stable and unstable;

The three worlds, the three Vedas, the triple knowledge, the three fires,
the three luminaries, the social classes, and likewise dharma and the other two.
The three qualities (guṇas), the three castes (varṇas), the three gods,

But this supreme, indescribable state rests upon the half-mora;

This supreme form of yours is that which cannot be described by me;

He who knows the manifestation of various powers and who manifests various powers;
from bliss to bliss, from great bliss to supreme bliss, his form consists of the qualities of reality.
Thus, O Goddess, everything— both the manifest (*sakala*) and the unmanifest (*niṣkala*),
that Brahman which abides in non-duality and that which is established in duality— is pervaded by you.

O Goddess, whatever objects are eternal and whatever others perish; whatever objects are gross and likewise subtle; whether they be on earth, in the atmosphere, or elsewhere—from you alone is their attainment.

Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Having heard these words of the wise Mārkaṇḍeya, the sage Uṣas—

Therein are thousands of sacred fords frequented by the sages;

and bathing in them is declared to grant liberation, even for one who has performed evil deeds.
Those who remember the sacred fords, propitiate the deities,
bathe with faith, and possess conviction, they go to the supreme goal.

The region between the two divine rivers, the Sarasvatī and the Dṛṣadvatī,

"Even though I am far away, I go to Kurukṣetra and I dwell there"—

And there, bathing in that very lake while standing on the bank of the Sarasvatī, the knowledge consisting of Brahman will arise for him; of this there is no doubt.
The gods, seers, and perfected beings constantly frequent Kurujāṅgala;
by constantly frequenting it, one perceives Brahman within oneself.
For those who, having attained this fickle human state, desire liberation,
even if they are self-restrained, they may yet perform evil deeds.
Freed from the impurities arising from many births,
they behold the stainless, eternal God dwelling within the heart.
Kurukṣetra is the sacrificial altar of Brahmā, and the Sānnihita lake is meritorious.
There is fear of falling due to the passage of time for the planets, lunar mansions, and stars;
however, for those who have died at Kurukṣetra, no such falling occurs.
There, the gods headed by Brahmā, the ṛṣis, siddhas, cāraṇas,
gandharvas, apsarases, and yakṣas dwell, seeking that station.
Having gone there and bathed at the great pool of Sthāṇu with faith, one obtains whatever desire is conceived in the mind; of this there is no doubt.

and having reached Rantuka, he asked for forgiveness again and again.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Śrī Vāmana Purāṇa, in the section on the Greatness of Sara.
The sages said: "Tell us of the seven forests and the nine rivers that are remembered."

Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Listen, here in the middle of Kurukṣetra, there are seven forests whose names are meritorious and which remove all sins.
And the meritorious Kāmyaka forest, as well as the great Āditi-forest,
the meritorious forest of Vyāsa, and indeed the Phalaki-forest.
Therein is the Sūryavana grove, as well as the great Madhuvana;
and the sacred Śītavana, which destroys all impurities.
O twice-born ones, hear from me about these seven forests and the rivers:
the sacred river Sarasvatī and likewise the river Vaitaraṇī.
And the river of great merit, the Gaṅgā; the river Mandākinī;
the Madhusrāvā; the Vasunadī; and the Kauśikī, which destroys all evil.
The highly meritorious Dṛṣadvatī and likewise the river Hiraṇvatī—
all these rivers that flow only during the rainy season— except for the Sarasvatī.

The water of these rivers is proclaimed to be meritorious during the rainy season; they never experience the state of being "menstruating" (unfit for ritual use). Indeed, by the power of the sacred ford (*tīrtha*), these excellent rivers are truly meritorious.
Let the sages listen with pleasure to the fruit of bathing at sacred fords;
both the journey there and the mere remembrance of it destroy all impurities.
And having seen the mighty gatekeeper Rantuka,
the man should salute the Yakṣa and then undertake his journey across the river.
From there, O Brahmins, one should go to the great forest named Ādityavana,
where Aditi performed severe and great penance for the sake of obtaining sons.
Having bathed there and beheld Aditi, the mother of the gods,
one gives birth to a heroic son who is free from all defects;
he ascends a celestial chariot (vimāna) that resembles a hundred suns.
From there, O best of Brahmins, one should go to the unsurpassed abode of Viṣṇu,
renowned by the name Savana, where Hari is ever present.
Having bathed in the Vimale and beheld Vimaleśvara,
a man goes to the stainless heaven and proceeds to the world of Rudra.
Seeing Hari and Baladeva together in one place, filled with fear, one attains liberation from the defilements born of the Kali age.
From there, one should go to the Pāriplava tīrtha, renowned throughout the three worlds;
having bathed there and beheld Brahmā accompanied by the Vedas, [one attains merit].
Having obtained the fruit of the Brahmaveda, one shall attain the stainless heaven;
and having reached the confluence at Kauśikī, which is the source of sacred fords,
a man who bathes at that confluence attains the supreme state.
Having reached the sacred ford on earth that liberates one from all sins,
a man who bathes there while endowed with patience attains the supreme state.
Whatever offenses have been committed by a person against the earth,
all of them are forgiven for that embodied being as soon as he has bathed.
Then, having gone to Dakṣāśrama and beheld Śiva as Dakṣeśvara,
a human being obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Then, O best of the twice-born, having gone to Śālūkinī and bathed at that sacred ford,
one who worships Hari joined with Hara with devotion attains the worlds of those possessed of eyes, freed from all sins.
Having reached Sarpirdadhi, the supreme sacred ford of the Nāgas,
a man who performs an ablution there shall be liberated from the fear of serpents.
Then, O best of brahmins, one should go to Rantuka, the gatekeeper;
having stayed there for one night and bathed in that auspicious, excellent tīrtha.

having fed the Brāhmaṇas, one should prostrate and ask for their forgiveness.
"By your grace, O Lord of Yakṣas, I am liberated from my sins;

Having bathed at that sacred ford and beheld Hara Koṭīśvara,
a man endowed with constant faith obtains the merit of the five great sacrifices.

and having bathed there as well, a person shall indeed obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Having reached the Tīrtha of the Aśvins, the man who is endowed with faith and has conquered his senses becomes a possessor of beauty and shall be renowned for his glory.

having bathed there with faith, one attains the supreme state.

a human being obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.

Having consumed curd on Mount Yugandhara and dwelt in the abode of Acyuta,
you likewise wish to dwell with your sons after bathing in Bhūtālaya.
"I have told you this by day; at night I shall certainly devour you.

She spoke with a piteous voice, "O beautiful lady, show me favor.

When an eclipse of the sun occurs at some time,
having bathed then at Saṃnihatyā, you shall go to heaven purified.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, on the Greatness of Sara, in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.

Then, the best of the twice-born who frequents sacred fords should go to Rāmahrada.
Wherein [the city was destroyed] by the brahmin Rāma, who possessed blazing splendor and acted with speed.
"Having exterminated the kṣatriyas, that hero established five lakes;
we have heard, O tiger among men, that he filled them with blood."
By him the ancestors were thus gratified, as were the grandfathers;
then those ancestors, being pleased, spoke to Rāma, O best of the twice-born.
"O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed Bhārgava! We are pleased with you, O Lord, because of this devotion to your father and because of your prowess."
"Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—what do you desire, O one of great renown?
Thus addressed by his ancestors, Rāma, the supreme lord, [replied].

"By the grace of my father, I wish for my ascetic power to be restored once more;
and [I wish to atone] for that kṣatriya power which was destroyed by me when I was overcome by greed."
"Then, by your power, may I indeed be released from this sin;
and may these lakes become sacred fords (tīrtha) renowned upon the earth."

yet that which was done by you while overcome by anger—the extermination of the Kṣatriyas—"

"Having thus granted these boons— the fulfillment of his heart's desires and eternal residence in heaven— Rāma’s ancestors then [departed], O brahmins."

such are the meritorious lakes of Rāma belonging to the high-souled Bhārgava.

Having reached that sacred ford (tīrtha) renowned throughout the three worlds, which purifies the body, one who bathes there attains purification of the physical frame; of this there is no doubt.

for so long do the perfected ones (*siddhas*), devoted to sacred sites (*tīrtha*), wander among them,
until they attain here that sacred site which purifies the body.
Having immersed his body at that sacred ford with a restrained mind,
he attains the supreme state from which he does not return again.
O best of Brahmins, one should then go to the sacred ford renowned throughout the three worlds.
Therein all the worlds were uplifted by the powerful Viṣṇu.
Having attained the upliftment of the world and being intent on the remembrance of the sacred ford,
one who has bathed in that best of tīrthas beholds the eternal worlds.
Where Viṣṇu is eternally present and the eternal god Śiva resides,
one may attain liberation by propitiating those two gods through prostration.
From there, one should go to the most excellent Śrītīrtha at Śālagrāma;
the Goddess always grants her presence to one who has bathed there.

one should bathe there and worship the deities as well as the ancestors.

Having seen Śiva, who is worshipped by the ṛṣis, one attains liberation;
and having reached Sūryatīrtha and bathed there with a restrained mind, [one likewise attains it].
Having honored the ancestors and the gods and being devoted to fasting,
one attains the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and goes to the world of the Sun.

Gaṇapati himself stands at that entrance to the cave;

Having reached the Saṅginī, a sacred ford that is the refuge of liberation,
a man who bathes in the Tīrtha of the Goddess obtains supreme beauty.

having enjoyed vast pleasures, he reaches the supreme state.
Having bathed in Brahmāvarta, a man endowed with the knowledge of Brahman becomes so;
of this there is no doubt, and he may relinquish his life-breaths at his own will.
Then, O best of Brahmins, one should go to Rantuka, the gatekeeper;
there is the sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) on the Sarasvatī belonging to that high-souled lord of the Yakṣas.

O great brahmins, that sacred ford there is immense and difficult to find elsewhere;

and there is another great and excellent sacred ford (tīrtha) there called Svānulomāyana.

having bathed there with devotion, one obtains that very same fruit.

therefore, being full of faith and free from envy, bathe in this tīrtha.

then, having bathed, they all went to heaven with purified bodies."

Bharadvāja, Gautama, Jamadagni, Kaśyapa,

and as he contemplated creation, he was deluded by the quality of passion (rajas).
