tormented by grief and pained by his suffering, he spoke: "This man is utterly enveloped by terrible sin. (Vamśastha 26.44)
"I shall perform the expiation as the deities shall instruct me.
Then all those deities spoke these words: [VamPSm 26.45]
Having bathed repeatedly at sacred fords, sprinkle yourself with water as far as the Sarasvatī flows against the current, even up to a mouthful of its power.
Having bathed with faith, a person attains liberation;
yet this man is solely intent on nourishing himself and devoted to reviling the gods.
Abandoned by the Brahmins, he is never purified;
therefore, having bathed with devotion at sacred fords (tīrthas) dedicated to him, [one should perform the rites].
"Consecrate him with water; then he will become purified.
Having heard these words, he then constructed a hermitage for him.
The king set out on a pilgrimage to sacred fords, intending to visit his own father Janaka;
day after day, he performed ritual ablutions at those holy sites.
He constantly consecrated his own father with the water of sacred fords;
at that very time, however, a dog arrived.
In the monastery of Sthāṇu, he was the head of the community and the guardian of the deity’s property;
he was always the protector of the wealth belonging to the religious establishment.
And he was beloved among all his kinsmen, being devoted to the service of the gods;
while he was thus conducting himself, remaining established on the path of dharma.

When his mind was moved by the destruction of the property of the gods at the appointed time, Yama, seeing him joined with that unrighteousness after he had gone to the next world, spoke these words: "Enter the womb of a dog; do not delay! (26.54)
Immediately after those words, tomorrow indeed, [he] was born in the Saugandhika forest.
Then, after a long time, surrounded by a pack of dogs,
he was humiliated by Saramā and overwhelmed by great suffering.
Having abandoned the holy Dvaitavana forest, he went to the Sānnihitya lake;
and as soon as he had entered it, by the very grace of Sthāṇu, [he was transformed].
Overcome by extreme thirst, he plunged into the Sarasvatī;
having bathed his body there, he was liberated from all sins.
Then, out of greed for food, he entered the small hut;
seeing the dog entering at that moment, he was overcome with fear.
He touched him gently and immersed him at Sthāṇutīrtha,
as he fell into the previous bathing places, sprinkling them with droplets.
He was sprinkled with drops of water produced from the dog's body,
and thereafter he became dispassionate through his gaze upon the dog and its subsequent death.
By the greatness of Sthāṇu-tīrtha, he was delivered by his son;
becoming composed at that very moment, he began to offer praise.
Vena said:
"I take refuge in you, the divine Lord Īśāna, the unborn one adorned with the moon,
the Great God, the Great-Souled One, the Master of the entire universe."
Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, destroyer of all enemies;
O Lord of the gods, who supports Bali and is worshipped by both gods and daityas.
O Virūpākṣa, Sahasrākṣa, Tryakṣa, beloved of the Lord of Yakṣas!
You whose hands and feet extend everywhere, and whose eyes, heads, and faces are on all sides.
Possessing ears everywhere in the world, you stand encompassing all;
O Śaṅkukarṇa of great deeds, whose abode is the ocean of Kumbhakarṇa!
O Gajendrakarṇa, Gokarṇa, Pāṇikarṇa, homage be to you!
O Śatajihva, Śatāvarta, Śatodara, Śatānana!
The singers of the Gāyatrī hymn sing of you, and those who offer praise with the *arka* hymns worship you;
O Śatakratu, they regard you as Brahmā, like a lofty pillar.
For in you, O Great Form, all the oceans, the clouds,
and likewise all the deities reside here within this body, like cows in a cow-pen.
In your body, I behold Soma, Agni, the Lord of Waters,
as well as Nārāyaṇa, Sūrya, Brahmā, and Bṛhaspati.
The Blessed One is the cause, the effect, and indeed the instrument of action;
he is the origin and the dissolution, as well as both the existent and the non-existent deity.
Homage to Bhava and Śarva, the bestower of boons who possesses a fierce form;
homage to the slayer of the Asura Andhaka and to the Lord of Creatures (Paśupati).
Salutation be to you, O destroyer of Tripura, who have three matted locks, three heads, and a trident held in your hand; who have three eyes and are the lord of the three worlds.
Homage to the shaven-headed one, to the fierce one, to the egg, the cause of origination;
homage to you, the shaven-headed one whose hand is occupied with a ḍiṇḍima drum.
Salutations to you with upward-pointing hair and fangs, to the emaciated and the deformed;
salutations to you who are smoke-colored, red, and black, and to the blue-necked one.
Homage be to the peerless one, to the deformed one, and to Śiva;
to him who wears a garland of suns, to Sūrya, who is garlanded with the banner of his own form.
Homage to you who transcend pride; homage to you who are most acute!
Homage to the Lord of the hosts, whose shoulders are like a bull’s and who wields the bow!
Homage to the one who thunders, to the fierce one, and to him who holds a vessel of leaves;
homage to the golden-hued one, homage to the one of golden splendor.
Homage to you who have been praised, who are worthy of praise, and who are the locus of praise; homage be to you, the All, the consumer of all, whose body is all beings.
Homage to the invoker and the slayer, who possesses a white, lofty banner;
homage to the one worthy of being bowed to and to the one who bows; homage also to Kaṭakaṭa.
Homage be to the one who has destroyed the afflictions, whether he be lying down or risen,
standing or running, shaven-headed or crooked.
Homage to the one whose nature is dancing, who excels in rhythm and musical instruments;
to the one who longs for the offering of dramatic performance, who excels in facial expressions and vocal instruments.
Homage to the eldest, to the most excellent, to the destroyer of strength and supreme power,
to the annihilator of time, to Time itself, whose form is the exhaustion of saṃsāra.
O beloved of the daughter of Himavat, homage be to you, Bhairava;
homage always to the Fierce One, and homage be to the Ten-armed One.
To him who is fond of funeral ashes, whose hand rests upon a skull-bowl,
who is terrifying and formidable, and who maintains fearsome vows.
Homage to the one with the distorted face; homage to the one with the fierce gaze of a corpse;
to the one greedy for raw and cooked meat, and to the one who loves the tambī lute.
Homage to the tree marked by the bull, homage to him who is resounded by the bellowing of bulls;
homage to Kaṭaṅkaṭa, to Bhīma, and to Paraparāyaṇa.
Homage to the most excellent one, the supreme one, the bestower of boons;
homage to him who is both detached and impassioned, who possesses meditative cultivation and a rosary of beads.
Salutation to the one who is divided by both difference and non-difference, to the shadow and to the sun;
to the one whose form is both non-terrible and terrible, and to the one who is more terrible than the most terrible.
Homage to Śiva, the peaceful; homage to you who are most profoundly peaceful, O you of many eyes and skulls, you of single form—homage be to you!
Homage to the one who is small, to the greedy, and to him who delights in sacrificial portions;
homage to the prince of Pañcāla, to the white-bodied one, and to the restrainer of self-control.
Homage to Citrorughanta, who rings with the sound of bell upon bell;
to him who possesses a hundred thousand bells, adorned with a garland of bells.
Homage to her who takes pride in the collision of the *praṇava*, to the one fond of *kilikili* cries;
to the one whose sound is *huṃ huṃ*, to Pārā, and to the one fond of the *huṃ huṃ* sound.
Homage to the one who is equal to all, who eternally dwells in the hollows of trees as his home,
who is like a jackal to the flesh of the womb, and who is both the Savior and the one who enables crossing.
Homage to the sacrifice, to the sacrificer, to that which is offered, and to that which is presented;
to the bearer of the sacrifice, to the oblation, to that which is heated, and to the heater.
Salutations to you, O Payas; salutations to the Lord of the Tuṇḍas;
salutations to the giver of food, the Lord of food, who partakes of various kinds of food.
Homage to the one with a thousand heads and a thousand feet,
to the one with a thousand uplifted tridents and a thousand ornaments.
Salutation to the protector of the followers of the child, who sports with the playfulness of a child;
salutation to the child, to the old man, to the agitated, and to the agitator.
Homage indeed to the one whose hair is stirred by the Ganges, to the one with hair like muñja grass;
homage to the one pleased by the six duties and devoted to the three duties.
Salutation to the naked one, to the fierce one, to the emaciated one, and to the one who causes bursting;
to the one who speaks of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, and to the one who is speech itself.

Salutation to the follower of Sāṃkhya, the foremost of the Sāṃkhyas, and the mouthpiece of Sāṃkhya-yoga; salutation to the one who is the charioteer for those without chariots, and whose chariot travels upon the fourfold path.
Salutations be to you, O Hari-keśa, who have a black antelope skin as an upper garment, a serpent as a sacred thread, and hair joined at the mouth;
to the Lord of Tryambikā and Ambikā, the unmanifest yet manifest Creator.

Salutations to the one who grants desires, who destroys desires, who wanders among the satisfied and the unsatisfied; salutations to the all-bestowing destroyer of sins, who contemplates for the duration of a kalpa.
O Great Being, O mighty-armed one, O one of great strength, homage be to you!
O Great Cloud, O one of great appearance, O Great Time, O one of great splendor!
Salutations to you, the lord of clouds, the cycles of the ages, and the moon and sun;
you are the food, the eater of food, the consumer of the ripened, and the supreme purifier.
The fourfold collection of living beings— those born from a womb, those born from an egg, those born from sweat, and those born from a sprout— are you alone, O Lord of the gods of gods.
O Brahman, the learned call you the creator of this world of moving and unmoving beings, its protector, and likewise its destroyer; they call you Brahman, the goal of those who know Brahman.
The proponents of Brahman say that you are the supreme light of the mind, that you are the wind among lights,
and that you are the bee in the tree of the *haṃsa*.
They say that you consist of the Yajus, the Ṛks, and likewise the Sāmans;
you are eternally recited by the multitudes of Vedas and Upaniṣads through hymns of praise.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those of lower castes—you alone are they;
you are the masses of clouds, the lightning, the thunderbolt, and the roar of thunder.
You are the year, the seasons, the month, and even half a month;
you are the ages (yugas), the moments (nimeṣas), the divisions of time (kāṣṭhās), the lunar mansions (nakṣatras), the planets, and the units of measure (kalās).
Among trees you are the *kakubha*, among mountains the Himavat mountain;
among beasts you are the tiger, among birds Tārkṣya, and among serpents Ananta.
Of oceans, he is the ocean of milk; of machines, the bow;
of weapons, the thunderbolt; and of vows, truth itself.
You alone are hatred and desire, passion and delusion, forgiveness and intolerance,
resolve and fortitude, greed, lust and anger, victory and defeat.

You are the bearer of the arrow, you are the wielder of the mace, and you are the bearer of the skull-topped staff and the bow; you are the cutter, the piercer, and the striker; you are the thinker, the leader, and the eternal one.
The Dharma endowed with the ten characteristics, as well as Artha and Kāma;
the oceans, rivers, the Gaṅgā, mountains, and lakes.
Climbing plants, creepers, grasses, herbs, domestic animals, wild beasts, and birds—
the undertaking of substances, actions, and qualities— yield flowers and fruits in due time.
The beginning and the end of the Vedas are likewise the Gāyatrī and the Praṇava;
[the fires] are red, green, blue, black, yellow, and white.
Kadru, Kapila, Kapota, and likewise Mecaka;
you alone are indeed Savarṇa and Avarṇa, the creator and the destroyer.
You are Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, Dhanada, and Anila;
you are Upaplava, Citrabhānu, and Svarbhānu as well.
The Śikṣāhaitra, the Trisauparṇa, the Śatarudriya of the Yajurveda,
and the Pavitra among purifiers— these are the most auspicious of all auspicious things.
The tinduka tree is born on the mountain; mudga is the life of all trees.
Vital breaths, goodness (sattva), passion (rajas), and darkness (tamas) are the lords of the first lunar day (pratipat).
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna;
as well as the opening and closing of the eyes, sneezing, and yawning.
With bloodshot eyes, a large mouth, and a protruding belly, he has pure hair, a tawny beard, and upward-pointing locks; he is both moving and unmoving.
One who knows song, instrumental music, and dance; one who is fond of song and instrumental music;
a fish, a net, and leeches; Time, the arts of play, and strife.
He is the untimely, the ill-timed, the evil time, and Time itself;
he is death, the maker of death, the yakṣa, and the one who strikes fear into the yakṣas.
Saṃvartaka, Antaka, Saṃvartakabalāhaka,
Ghaṇṭa, Ghaṇṭī, Māhaghaṇṭī, Cirī, Mālī, and Mātali.

He is the time of Brahmā, the fire of the end, the bearer of the staff, the shaven-headed one, and the wearer of three tufts of hair; he is the four ages, the four Vedas, and the promoter of the four sacrificial fires.
He is the leader of the four stages of life and likewise the creator of the four castes;
he is eternally fond of dice, a rogue, the presiding officer of the Gaṇas, and the lord of the Gaṇas.
Wearing red garlands and garments, Girika is the beloved of Girikā;
he is the craft itself, the best among artisans, and the originator of all crafts.
Bhaganetra, Aṅkuśa, Caṇḍa, the destroyer of Pūṣan’s teeth;
Svāhā, Svadhā, Vaṣaṭkāra, Namaskāra, and salutations again and again.
He whose vows are secret and whose austerities are hidden; he who is the savior and consists of salvation;
the sustainer, the ordainer, and the uniter; another who is the upholder of the earth.
He is Brahman, austerity, truth, the practice of vows, and straightforwardness;
he is the self of all beings, the creator of beings, prosperity, and the source of the past, the future, and the present.
Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svar, Ṛta, Dhruva, Dānta, Maheśvara,
Dīkṣita, Adīkṣita, Kānta, Durdānta, and Dāntasaṃbhava.
Candrāvarta, Yugāvarta, Saṃvartaka, and Pravartaka;
Bindu, Kāma, Aṇu, Sthūla, and Karṇikārasrajapriya.
Nandīmukha, Bhīmamukha, Sumukha, and likewise Durmukha;
Hiraṇyagarbha, Śakuni, Mahoragapati, and Virāṭ; Adharmahā, Mahādeva, Daṇḍadhāra, and Gaṇotkaṭa. // 26.136 //
Gonarda, Gopratāra, and Govṛṣeśvaravāhana.
The protector of the three worlds, Govinda, Gomārga, and Mārga;
Sthira, Śreṣṭha, Sthāṇu, Vikrośa, and Krośa.
He who is difficult to ward off, difficult to endure, difficult to withstand, and difficult to overcome;
he who is unassailable, difficult to perceive, difficult to behold, invincible, and victory itself.
He is cool like the moon and hot like fire; he is free from hunger, thirst, and disease;
he is the remover of mental anguish and physical ailments, the destroyer of all maladies.
The eternal God is the multitude and the destroyer of the multitude;
he is Śikhaṇḍin, the lotus-eyed one, whose abode is a forest of lotuses.
Tryambaka, Daṇḍadhāra, Ugradaṃṣṭra, Kulāntaka,
Viṣāpaha, Suraśreṣṭha, Somapa, O Lord of the Maruts!
You are the consumer of nectar, the protector of the world, the God of gods, and the Lord of the Gaṇas.
You are the honey-drinker of those dripping with honey; you are the speaker of Brahman, dripping with clarified butter;
you are the enjoyer of all worlds, the Grandfather of all worlds.
You alone are the golden-seeded Puruṣa; you are female, you are male, and indeed you are neuter.
You are the child, the youth, and the aged; you are the fang of the gods, our mountain, the creator of the universe, and the destroyer of the universe.
You are indeed the Ordainer, the most excellent among the creators of all; bowing down, they always worship you.
The moon and the sun are your two eyes, for you are indeed Agni and the Great-Grandfather.
By propitiating you, they obtain eloquence through Sarasvatī; you are the maker of day and night, and of the closing and opening of the eyes.
Neither Brahmā nor Govinda, nor those ancient seers,
O Śaṅkara, are able to know your majesty in its true essence.
Encompassing hundreds of thousands of men,
you always stand as their protector and thinker beyond the great darkness.

Salutation to that Self of Yoga, whom those who are sleepless, who have mastered their breath, who are established in purity, and whose senses are restrained, perceive as a light while practicing yoga.
And those subtle forms of yours which cannot be demonstrated—
by means of them, protect me constantly, as a father protects his own biological son.
Protect me, protect me; I am worthy of your protection, O Sinless One! Homage be to you!
The Blessed One is compassionate toward his devotees, and I am always devoted to you.
Salutation to that one whose self is Rudra, who always possesses matted hair and carries a staff, whose body is pot-bellied, and who has a water-pot and a quiver at his side.
Salutation to that one whose essence is water, in whose hair are the clouds, in whose every limb-joint are the rivers, and in whose belly are the four oceans.
I take refuge in that one who lies within the waters, having consumed all beings when the end of the age has arrived.
Entering the mouth of Rāhu, he who drinks the moon at night and swallows the sun—
the Kharbhānu— is protected by your splendor.
And those fetuses that have fallen here due to the Rakṣas of Rudragandha—homage be to you! O Khadhā, Svāhā! they attain that wonder.
May those persons, the size of a thumb, who reside within the bodies of all embodied beings, protect me always; may they indeed cause me to flourish.
Those who [dwell] in rivers, in oceans, on mountains, and in caves;
at the roots of trees, in cow-pens, and in the depths of dense forests.
At crossroads, on carriage roads, at squares, and in assembly halls;
in elephant, horse, and chariot stables, and in ruined gardens and dwellings.

And those who are within the five elements, in the cardinal and intermediate directions, those situated between the moon and the sun, and those within the rays of the moon and the sun; VamPSm_26.159 //
To those who have gone to the subterranean realm (rasātala) and to those who have gone beyond that,
homage to them, homage to them, and homage to them forever!
To those Rudras for whom there is no number, no measure, and no form— homage be to them, who are in incalculable hosts, forever.
Be gracious to me; may it be well with you, for my heart is fixed upon your being.
O Lord, my heart is in you; my intellect and my mind are in you.
Having thus praised Mahādeva, that best of the twice-born ceased speaking.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, on the Greatness of Sara, in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the god Bhava, the lord of the three worlds, spoke to him.
And the master of speech uttered for him this supreme utterance, which brings consolation.
"O King of noble vows, I am truly pleased with this hymn of yours!
What need is there for further words? You shall dwell in my presence."
After dwelling for a very long time, you shall once again be born from my body as an asura named Andhaka, the destroyer of the gods.
Having taken birth in the house of Hiraṇyākṣa, you will attain growth due to your former, terrible karma consisting of the reviling of the Vedas.
When you shall become filled with longing for the Mother of the World, then,
having struck my body with a spear, I shall purify it for ten million years.
Having become free from blemish even there, and having praised me again with devotion,
he became renowned as a lord of the Gaṇas, remembered by the name Bhṛṅgiriṭi.
By remaining in my presence, you shall then attain perfection;
so too for whoever recites or hears this hymn proclaimed by Vena.
One shall not encounter anything inauspicious and shall attain a long life,
just as the Blessed Lord Śiva is preeminent among all the gods.
Likewise, this most excellent hymn, composed by Vena among all hymns,
has been proclaimed for the sake of fame, sovereignty, happiness, power, wealth, and honor.
It should be listened to with devotion and with effort by those desiring knowledge;
likewise by one who is diseased, suffering, wretched, or beset by fear of thieves and kings.
Or, being freed from royal duties, one is liberated from great fear;
indeed, with this very body, one shall attain the preeminence among the Gaṇas.
Endowed with splendor and fame, he becomes stainless;
neither Rākṣasas nor Piśācas, nor Bhūtas nor Vināyakas [can harm him].
Obstacles shall arise in that house where this hymn is recited;
however, a woman who hears this hymn after having obtained permission from her husband [shall not suffer such obstacles].
Whether on the mother’s side or the father’s side, she becomes as worthy of worship as a deity;
whoever, with a concentrated mind, should hear this divine hymn or recite it, [shall obtain great merit].
All his undertakings constantly reach fulfillment—
whatever is conceived by the mind and whatever is proclaimed by speech.
Everything is accomplished for him by the recitation of this praise;
whatever sin has been committed through mind, deed, or speech is destroyed.
Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—whatever is desired by your heart.
Vena said: "By the majesty of this linga, and likewise by the sight of the linga,
I am indeed liberated from all sins through the sight of you."
"If you are pleased with me, O God, and if a boon is to be granted to me,
[then grant one for] this servant of yours who was born in the womb of a dog due to eating the property of a deity."
O Śaṅkara, you ought to show favor even to this one;
it was out of fear of him that I submerged myself in the middle of the lake.
"Previously, he was prevented by the gods from bathing at this sacred ford;
since he has rendered me this service, I choose [this boon] for his sake."
Having heard these words of his, Śaṅkara, being pleased, said:
"He too shall be liberated from sin; of this there is no doubt."
By my grace, O mighty-armed one, he shall go to the world of Śiva;
likewise, having heard this hymn, one is liberated from all sins.
O lord of the earth, by hearing the majesty of Kurukṣetra, of this lake,
and the origin of my liṅga, one is liberated from sins.
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, who is honored by all the worlds,
vanished right there while all the worlds were looking on.
And that dog, at that very moment, remembering his former birth,
assumed a divine form and appeared before the king.
Having performed his ablutions, Vainya, longing for the sight of his father,
saw an empty hut at Sthāṇutīrtha and was overcome with grief.
Seeing him, Vena, filled with great joy, spoke these words:
"O child, by you, a true son, I have been saved from the ocean of hell."
Constantly consecrated by you and stationed on the sandy bank of a sacred ford,
he has attained this through the grace of this holy man and from the vision of the god Sthāṇu.
"Having been freed from sin, I shall go to the heavenly world where Śiva resides.
Having spoken thus, he established Maheśvara facing the king.
He attained perfection at Sthāṇu-tīrtha, having been delivered by that son;
and that dog also attained supreme perfection through the power of Sthāṇu-tīrtha.
Liberated from all impurities,
the king, having protected the earth, went to the abode of Bhava, freed from his ancestral debts.
Having procreated sons in accordance with the Dharma, having performed unimpeded sacrifices,
having given desired gifts to the Brahmins, and having enjoyed various kinds of pleasures;
Then, having freed his friends from debts and satisfied his wives with their desires,
the king anointed his son in the kingdom and departed for Kurukṣetra.
Having performed severe austerities there and having worshipped Śaṅkara,
he cast off his body by his own will and departed for the supreme state.
The man who hears of this power of the holy site of Sthāṇu,
being liberated from all sins, goes to the supreme goal.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter in the Śrī Vāmana Purāṇa, in the section on the Greatness of Sara.
